anchors.paper_title: Temporal structure of item presentation modulates brain oscillations in verbal working memory
anchors.reason: Same authors, 30 adults, seven digits in four presentation modes (Simultaneous, Fast, Slow, Fast+delay) match the dataset; the paper reports EEG from this data (IsSupplementTo).

metadata.methods_description: EEG (64 channels), ECG and PPG were recorded in BrainVision format. Resting state comprised four 1-minute blocks of eyes-closed and eyes-open rest followed by about 4 minutes of cartoon watching. In the working memory task, participants saw seven-digit sequences in four presentation modes (simultaneous 2800 ms; fast sequential 400 ms per digit; fast with 600 ms ISI; slow sequential 1000 ms per digit) and typed the digits in order on a numpad. Trial-wise accuracy and partial-score measures were computed.

citation_details.title: Impact of mindfulness-based strategy training on working memory in twice-exceptional students in Saudi Arabia
citation_details.author: B. M. Alotaibi, Sarah Abdullah Al-Rashidi, Atef Abdallah Bahrawi
citation_details.abstract: Introduction . One of the most challenging tasks for a teacher is addressing the needs of students with twice-exceptionality, whose conflicting characteristics complicate the learning process. Implementing new strategies to foster a positive emotional environment and mitigate negative experiences for this group of students represents a promising approach that can enhance existing methods of positive psychology. Aim. This research aims to investigate the impact of mindfulness-based cognitive interventions on the efficiency of working memory in twice-exceptional Saudi middle school students. Methodology and research methods. The study involved the development of mindfulness strategies among the participants, followed by in-depth interviews to evaluate their perceptions of the results obtained. citation_details.title: Temporal Structure of Item Presentation Modulates Brain Oscillations in Verbal Working Memory
citation_details.author: Alexandra I. Kosachenko, Danil I. Syttykov, Dmitry Tarasov, Alexander I. Kotyusov, Dauren Kasanov, Sergey B. Malykh, Boris Kotchoubey, Yuri G. Pavlov
citation_details.abstract: Previous studies of verbal working memory (WM) have reported inconsistent changes in alpha power during retention, with both increases and decreases observed. We asked whether these discrepancies arise from how stimuli are presented. Thirty adults memorized seven digits presented in four modes: Simultaneous (all digits for 2800 ms) or sequential presentations at Fast (400 ms per digit), Slow (1000 ms per digit), and Fast + delay (400 ms per digit plus a 600-ms free time in between). We analyzed EEG during encoding and a 6-s retention period in theta (4-7 Hz), alpha (8-13 Hz), and beta (18-24 Hz) frequency bands. Encoding produced parametric load-related theta increase and beta decrease, possibly reflecting growing executive control demands and motor program formation, respectively. Alpha power did not scale with load during encoding. Single trial models linked stronger encoding theta and deeper alpha suppression to better recall, whereas retention power did not predict accuracy. During retention, theta and beta were unaffected by presentation mode. Alpha power did not differ significantly when all sequential modes were grouped together compared to the simultaneous mode. However, the Fast + delay mode uniquely showed below-baseline alpha in the first half of the retention. Our findings suggest that alpha dynamics are sensitive to the temporal structure of encoding and retention periods, particularly the presence or absence of free intervals between stimulus presentations. We propose that alpha modulation during WM retention may reflect processes beyond the simple gating of irrelevant sensory information.

citation_details.title: Predicting Cognitive Tasks from Single-Channel EEG through Task-Semantic Alignment
citation_details.author: Ryota Kanai C
citation_details.abstract: Studies of data scaling in electroencephalography (EEG) and related noninvasive recordings suggest that simple wearable devices could eventually reveal more about cognitive states. However, publicly available EEG data are difficult to combine. Different laboratories record different tasks, participants, and devices. Task-agnostic self-supervised learning can exploit such data, but representations learned only with EEG signals have not consistently produced feature representations that are directly effective for decoding the cognitive state. We therefore aimed to incorporate task information by embedding experimental instructions, stimuli and response demands in a common semantic space, and trained an EEG encoder to align signals from a single anterior--posterior differential channel with those task vectors. This framework supports zero-shot prediction without target-condition calibration and few-shot prediction using labeled samples. On a reserved ten-class evaluation, the highest observed zero-shot balanced accuracy was 30.13% (chance 10%). In a separate developmental few-shot experiment, balanced accuracy reached 34.47% using 16 labeled EEG examples per class from another participant, and 74.99% using examples from the test participant's own task recording. Our experiments suggest that training models on datasets with multiple tasks per participant appeared useful, whereas adding datasets containing only one or a few tasks sometimes reduced established performance despite broader task coverage. These exploratory results suggest that EEG datasets that repeat varied cognitive tasks and everyday activities within the same individuals across days, devices and independent studies would be particularly useful for training an EEG foundation model for predicting cognitive states.

citation_details.title: Rapid item-updating elevates neural manifold dynamics during encoding: evidence from a fixed-load verbal working-memory dataset
citation_details.author: Robin Langell
citation_details.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
citation_details.abstract: We analyzed open neuro dataset ds006848, a fixed-load verbal working-memory EEG-ECG-PPG dataset (N = 30), comparing four visual presentation modes. Rapid sequential encoding (Fast, FastDelay) elevated neural manifold mobility (m) and diffusivity (d) during encoding relative to simultaneous or slow-paced display — while recall accuracy showed the opposite ordering. This behavioral dissociation indicates that m/d indexes rapid item-updating demand, not encoding success. Maintenance-period geometry was indistinguishable across conditions (Friedman p = 0.96), confirming the effect is encoding-specific.
